It was attacked by the terrorists, and, under such circumstances, it was extremely difficult to work. As of March 2001 till the end of the year, we were extremely pressed with work, if I may say so, and not only with our regular activities. There were additional obligations for the Ministry of Interior, for the sector of internal affairs as part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regards to what you said, that you had insufficient material and human resources, tell me whether, in 2001, besides the regular police officers who were employed by the ministry in Skopje, were there any other persons called in?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: In view of the situation and in view of the human resources we had available, we could not respond to the tasks we were facing. Due to these reasons, the reserve forces of the Ministry of Interior was activated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we go on, because you mentioned the reservists now, those reservists that you called in pursuant, probably, to the law on the rule book - let's not go into that now - tell me whether the reserve forces were employed by the Ministry of Interior after they were called in? Did they become employed?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: No. They were not employed at the Ministry of Interior. If they were employed in other bodies or in other companies was stagnant and they received compensation on the part of the Ministry of Interior, that is to say, the budget of the Republic. I'm not expert on this topic, but I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Appreciating the fact that you are not expert in this area and that I probably need to ask these questions of someone else, but if you have experience from that time, could you tell me for someone to become a member of the reserve forces of the police, was it sufficient for a person to be issued with weapons and uniform, or were there any other requirements for this? If you know it, of course, answer it.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: As part of the sector for internal affairs, there is -- there was and there is a unit for defence preparations charged with topics such as these. According to my modest understanding - I will say again - weapons and uniform does not make a person a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will kindly ask you now to look at the document after tab 25. And before that, since you spoke about the situation in Skopje that lasted throughout 2001, tell me, what was the impact of the events in other parts of the Republic on to the situation in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Information about the rest of the Republic, the situation in the rest of the country, were received through the headquarters of the operative action Ramno. In regards to what I called as conflict, an operative action was formed named Ramno, the aim of which was to undertake measures and activities to follow movements and activities of terrorist groups in Macedonia. Within the framework of this operative action, operative headquarters was established at the ministry as well as in all SVRs - at that time there were 11 of them - and in the OVRs. Information was exchanged through headquarters which I mentioned, and according to the information I had available at the time, the northern part of the Republic towards Kosovo was under particular threat than Tetovo and Kumanovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And tell me now, in addition to those measures, such as establishment of the operative action Ramno, what was the reaction of the people to those various events, and did it make the situation in Skopje more complex?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: This is a very complex question. At the beginning of the crisis, we faced with a -- a very weak response of reservists. On the other hand, we faced a revolt among the citizens of the Republic of Macedonia who could not accept the fact that someone is setting their houses on fire, is expelling them from their homes, and they could not accept the fact that law enforcement forces of the Republic of Macedonia are undertaking measures which they deemed as insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you look now at the document that I asked you to see in tab 25. That is Exhibit 1D114. And you can see here that this is a decision to form a commission for determining the causes, number of participants, the aim, and the way of expression of the public protest of the citizens in front of the parliament of the Republic of Macedonia, held in the night between the 25th and the 26th of June, 2001. Tell me, do you have, Mr. Stojanovski, any knowledge about this event?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the problems that we had faced, I feel free to say, almost every day, although this was a bit more prominent or striking than the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present there when those events took place?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. And I was in front of the parliament of the Republic of Macedonia together with my co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we've already heard testimony about this event, tell me, please, what efforts and why were steps taken, if they were, by the police of the city of Skopje that evening?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: The situation was very complex, since the protesters were actually citizens and were accompanied, if I can say so, by police reservists, police officers, members of the army, who wanted to express their protest because of the events related to the village of Aracinovo. For clarification, immediately in the days before, actually, the Ministry of Interior took action to seize control over the village of Aracinovo and had clashes with the terrorists who were located there at that time. When the clashes started, an order was issued. I believe that it was an order issued by the president, the late president of the state, and probably pressured by the international public. The action was stopped, and we were forced to provide a corridor for -- to allow the terrorists to be taken out of the village, having their complete armament with them. Most of the citizens could not accept this, found this unacceptable so went out to protest, and they were joined by many of the police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovski. As I have already said, some witnesses have already testified about that. But what I'm interested in now is this: In view of the situation as it was, people with arms, protesting, the possibility of attacking the sobranje, parliament, what was the priority as far as the police were concerned? Did you have priority with respect to those events, that is to say, to disband the masses, to defend the sobranje, the assembly, or was something else a priority and -- that you acted upon that night?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: So the SVR Skopje had a certain capacity at the moment. Unfortunately, we were not able to perform our task fully with regards to the security for the parliament building, since, after the information on the protests before -- in front of the parliament building were spread, we simultaneously received information that part of the Albanian population in the settlement of Bit Pazar in Skopje, started to gather, and such information were going back and forth uncontrollably between the two sides. And at a given moment, it became somewhat expected that there would be a clash between the citizens who protested in front of the parliament building and the citizens who had already started gathering in the Bit Pazar settlement and the -- who were of Albanian ethnicity. At that moment, we needed to establish a priority, you understand, considering the limited resources, and we decided to attach primary importance to what was taking place in the Bit Pazar settlement or, actually, we decided that we must not allow an ethnic-based clash to take place. So part of the available resources were directed towards the stone bridge in Skopje and we tried to secure the both sides, groups of citizens to prevent a direct clash between them. I believe that, unless we did that, there would have been much graver consequences in the Republic of Macedonia. So this is why we failed to complete our task before the parliament building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So if I have understood you correctly, and to avoid asking a leading question and upsetting my learned friend, your decision that night was to protect the parts of town inhabited by the Albanian population, to prevent an ethnic conflict from breaking out. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: You can realistically say that the number of Macedonian citizens was far greater than the number of citizens of Albanian ethnicity, and I think that if we had allowed that group of people to go to the other side of the settlement, that there would have been many, many people injured. We simply could not allow this to happen, so we needed to protect that population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that there were -- was the reserve police force there and the army and that the citizens joined in later on. Tell me now, please, do you know of a measure that was taken by the minister of the interior after that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: There was a measure taken, but to be honest, the result was not something really. Namely, the minister issued a decision to disband the reserve force. However, that decision was later suspended by the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that comes after tab 18. It is 1D90, Exhibit 1D90. And that is page 1D4036 in Macedonian; and in English it is 1D4038.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: I apologise, 4036?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And -- part of that document, that is to say, underneath the three stars, the heading there is demobilisation of the reserve force, reserve composition. It says: "The minister of internal affairs Ljube Boskoski, at a press conference stated that members of the reserve force of the Republic of Macedonia will be demobilised and withdrawn from the check-points around Skopje." Now is that the decision that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: I believe that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the next document after tab 19. And it is Exhibit 1D91; page 1D4041 in Macedonian, and 1D4042 in the English. On that page, we have a text that says the following: "The police reservists are returning to the check-points." And it says that: "The Ministry of Interior withdrew the decision for demobilisation of the reserve police force and ordered a remobilisation which will be put into effect selectively. The remobilisation of the reserve police force shall be conducted upon the request of the commander of the chief of the Macedonian Armed Forces Boris Trajkovski, due to the security situation in the country." Now, is that the decision which you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the clock, and I don't know how you intend to work today. I understood it that we would be working for two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And there's another quarter of an hour to go in the second session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking of the morning sittings, so that was my mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Stojanovski, you were speaking about the formation of the Ramno staff which had the task of collecting information and data on the situation in the territory, and I'd like to ask you now to take a look at the following document. It comes after tab 22. It is Exhibit P387 -- I'm sorry, 381. It's Exhibit P381. It's a decision on the formation of the Ramno Operative Action Headquarters. The date is 2001, the 20th of May. Are you familiar with this document, or let me put it this way, do you know that the headquarters was formed?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document, but I know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: -- I am not familiar with the document, but I know the names because I was in the headquarter of the SVR Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at another document now it is 1D112, after tab 21. 1D4304 in Macedonian, the page number; and in English it is 1D4306, in English. This is, once again, a document on the formation of the Ramno Operative Action Headquarters, and the date is the 7th of March, 2001. Tell me, please, do you know when this Ramno Operative Action was recorded and registered and who the minister was?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: I believe that the action was registered in the month of March, and the -- Mrs. Dosta Dimovska was the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the gathering of information about this, tell me, who assessed the security situation in a given area?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, the entire situation caused the need to have constant and continuing assessment of the securing situation, and that was a duty that belonged to the OVRs, considering the fact that, of course, since they were working, covering a given territory, they were the best placed to know the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about assessment and evaluation in the internal affairs department, was it their duty to send their assessment to the internal affairs sector of Skopje, and did the sector itself evaluate the situation, as far as the city of Skopje was concerned?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The sector for internal affairs collected the security assessments, so to say, and the entirety of them formed the security assessment for the city. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you just said, in view of the fact that there was a crisis on and there was the need to assess the security situation, in that regard were any other measures taken in order to be able to control the area, in operative terms?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: After the security assessment of the situation was made, and aiming towards performing the tasks indicated, enumerated in the operative action Ramno, the OVRs started operating in a check-point-based manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was responsible for establishing the number of -- or, rather, who decided where the check-points were going to be and how many of them there were to be erected in the territory of the city of Skopje?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: As I previously stated, they were the ones who knew the situation on the ground best. Upon a proposal coming from the commanders of police stations, the head of the OVR approved -- or actually passed the plan for the erecting and the dimensions of the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the next document, which comes after tab 10. It is 65 ter 1D1238. Here we have an order for performing service. This should -- this is a draft translation, in fact. If we have it on e-court I can proceed; if not, then I would like to deal with it later. Or perhaps I can go on with another question. We'll come back to this later on. I see it's come up on e-court. I didn't know if the translation was ready yet. Anyway, Mr. Stojanovski, we have here an order, an order that must be acted upon. Now in addition to the check-points that you spoke about earlier on, were other measures resorted to on the part of the police in order to be able to deal with the crisis that you were faced with?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is proof that, in addition to check-point-based work there were also motor patrols and of course infantry patrols or our so-called local patrol police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about check-points a moment ago you said that the -- it was up to the police station to propose this measure and the chief to allow it to go ahead. You told us how many check-points there were and so on. But was it possible at all to change the number of check-points and their locations in a given area, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Depending on the current security situation in that area, the head of the OVR and upon a proposal of the police station commander was able to change the location of the check-point or the composition and the number of the officers serving the check-point. Now, regarding this, I had nothing to do -- I had no influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: I received the information from the operative headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether the SVR of Skopje had certain duties in determining the number of check-points, who manned the check-points, how many there were and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: No, the SVR Skopje had no competence there. Still, however, the OVR had the duty to inform the headquarters of the SVR Skopje. This was due to organisational reasons only, so that we know how many people are deployed there and where are they deployed and of course to provide some logistics, if needed, or rendering assistance to a certain check-point if such need would arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the MVR, the Ministry of the Interior, at the level of the Republic of Macedonia? Did it have any duties and responsibilities linked to those check-points, where their location was, how many of them there were, and their establishment in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: No. I think that through the headquarters of the SVR Skopje the MOI was informed through so-called summary information only about the number of check-points and the number of persons deployed there, without details.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at the order itself. The number is 2456. And I'd like to ask you, since you mentioned a moment ago when you spoke about certain activities and operative control, can you tell me what this means: Operative control, in the police sense? What does it actually mean and imply?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: The operative control is explained and applied pursuant to an instructive act of the Ministry of Interior. Those are measures and activities undertaken by the authorised officers in cases when there are -- there is general knowledge that crimes are perpetrated somewhere, or that perpetrators of crimes are gathering. This operative control could be aiming at persons, at locations or facilities, buildings. This presupposes following -- direct following of the events, monitoring the events in the vicinity of those facilities or locations, or check-points. It also presupposes provisional controls, occasional controls of persons and asking them for their ID. And the operative control could end in cases when, once it is established that the reasons for its establishment had terminated, it could be terminated by being converted into operative processing or by filing a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, if you look at this order and the description of the action to be undertaken as stipulated in this order, control of catering establishments, to tour the various premises where criminals acts had been committed and so on and so forth, to also apprehend the persons wanted by court warrant, et cetera, tell me, do these actions actually mean practical implementation of what you were speaking about and which is called operative control in the police vocabulary?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The items 1 and 3 could be considered as such, this means that the police officers were given tasks within a registered operative control or an established operative control. These are some of the measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps just one more question before we break. You have explained to us what operative or operational control means in the police sense and how it was put into practice. This concept of operative control in the police sense, does it have anything at all to do with operative control as used in the army?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI
utterances.text: There is no basis for the comparison. They are completely different notions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. The reasons have been discussed. We will limit ourselves to two sessions, each of a full one-and-a-half hours, so ending now today and tomorrow. We will continue the hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00, and attempt to sit for two full one-and-a-half hour sessions, subject to the continuing comfort of the witness. So we adjourn now and resume at 9.00 in the morning.
